risks.note: Listed by the Company itself among its major risks. The Group states it is exposed to credit risk from operating activities, primarily trade receivables, plus loans receivable, investments and other financial instruments. Structurally acute for a staffing business that carries a large receivable book against a small number of large industrial clients: the segment note discloses that the single largest customer accounted for a double-digit share of total revenue in each of the last two years. Trade receivables are by far the largest financial asset on the Group's books.

Company-flagged. Manpower demand is derived demand: a cyclical slowdown in capex by infrastructure, energy and industrial sectors, delays in EPC, oil & gas, manufacturing or renewable-energy projects, and slow client decision-making all translate directly into deployment gaps. Management explicitly links global geopolitical tension and commodity volatility to delayed capital expenditure and moderated hiring activity.
risks.risk: Cyclicality of client capital expenditure and project execution timelines

risks.note: Company-flagged, and the sharpest structural risk for the model since the deployable engineer is the product. Demand for engineering, renewable energy, AI, semiconductor, digital and GCC talent is stated to outpace availability; the widening skill gap may intensify competition for qualified professionals, raise hiring costs and lengthen recruitment cycles.
risks.risk: Talent acquisition, retention and skill-gap risk

risks.note: Company-flagged on both sides of the spread. The organised staffing industry faces intense competition from domestic, multinational and technology-enabled recruitment firms causing pricing pressure, while rising employee costs and inflationary pressures push the cost base up. This is a structural squeeze in a business whose largest single cost line is employee benefits.
risks.risk: Margin compression from competitive intensity and rising employee costs

risks.note: Company-flagged. AI, automation and digital technologies may reduce demand for routine and repetitive roles even as they raise demand for high-skilled professionals. Management states staffing companies must continuously adapt talent strategies, technology capabilities and recruitment processes; failure to do so is an existential risk to a deputation-volume model.
risks.risk: AI-led workforce disruption and technology obsolescence

risks.note: Company-flagged. Changes in labour regulations, employment law, taxation, social security requirements and compliance frameworks directly alter workforce management economics and raise compliance obligations for staffing companies and their clients. A staffing intermediary bears this risk on behalf of its clients.

Company-flagged in the MD&A as forex fluctuations affecting international operations plus geopolitical developments in overseas markets. NOTE A CONTRADICTION IN THE AR: the Ind AS financial-risk note asserts 'The Group does not have significant foreign currency exposure and hence is not exposed to any significant foreign currency risks', yet the same note discloses unhedged foreign-currency trade receivables outstanding at March 31, 2026 in USD, GBP, QAR and SAR, and separately states there were NO derivative instruments outstanding at either March 31, 2026 or March 31, 2025 - i.e. the exposure is entirely unhedged. With international expansion an explicit strategic priority, this risk is directionally increasing while the note describes it as insignificant.
risks.risk: Foreign exchange exposure and geopolitical risk in overseas markets

risks.note: Company-flagged, tied to digital operations and technology-enabled recruitment platforms. Management states it proactively updates digital verification systems to address emerging cybersecurity and compliance risks as industrial plants and GCC clients modernise. A staffing business holds large volumes of candidate and employee personal data, making this both an operational and a regulatory exposure.
